children.text: We are a small design studio focused on creating meaningful work for thoughtful clients. Founded in 2020, we've had the privilege of working with brands across technology, culture, and the arts.
Our approach is simple: listen carefully, think deeply, and craft with intention. We believe that good design is invisible — it gets out of the way and lets the work speak for itself.
What we do
We specialize in brand identity, web design, and art direction. Whether you need a complete visual identity or a single website, we bring the same level of care and attention to every project.

data.title: Meridian
data.summary: A complete brand identity for a creative collective bringing together artists and technologists.

children.text: Meridian Collective needed a visual identity that could bridge the gap between traditional art and emerging technology. The challenge was to create something that felt timeless yet forward-looking.
The approach
We developed a wordmark that combines classical typography with subtle geometric forms. The color palette draws from both digital interfaces and natural materials, creating a bridge between worlds.
The result

The new identity has been applied across print and digital touchpoints, from business cards to a fully responsive website. Meridian has received positive feedback from both artists and technologists alike.

data.title: Volta
data.summary: Website design for a renewable energy startup making clean power accessible to everyone.

children.text: Volta is on a mission to make renewable energy accessible to everyone. They needed a website that could explain complex technology simply while inspiring trust in potential customers.
Design principles
We focused on clarity and warmth. The design uses generous whitespace and a vibrant green accent that evokes growth and sustainability without feeling clichéd.

data.title: The Archive
data.summary: Exhibition catalog and print materials for a retrospective on modernist architecture.

children.text: The Archive was a major exhibition at the City Museum, showcasing 50 years of modernist architecture through photographs, drawings, and models. We designed the complete print identity.
The catalog
The 240-page catalog uses a strict grid system inspired by the work being exhibited. Full-bleed photography alternates with dense text spreads, creating a rhythm that echoes the exhibition layout.

data.title: Coastal
data.summary: A photographic study of the Pacific coastline, exploring the intersection of land, sea, and sky.

children.text: Coastal began as a weekend project and grew into a year-long exploration of the Pacific shoreline. Shot entirely on medium format film, the series captures the quiet drama of the coast.
Process

Each image was made at dawn or dusk, when the light is softest and the beaches are empty. The slow process of shooting film encourages patience and intentionality — qualities that show in the final work.

data.title: Blogfolio update: a new identity for a new season
data.excerpt: We refreshed our own identity this quarter — here is what changed and why we kept almost everything.

$media.alt: Sunlit studio workspace with two desks

children.text: Every few years we turn the lens on ourselves. This quarter it was our turn: a refreshed wordmark, a tighter type scale, and a site that finally matches how we actually work.
What changed
Less, mostly. We dropped two accent colours, merged three type styles into one, and rewrote every page of copy until each sentence earned its place.
A rebrand that removes things is usually the one that lasts.
The full case study will follow once the last of the collateral ships. Until then, the site you are reading is the release.

data.title: Designing with restraint
data.excerpt: Restraint is not the absence of ideas — it is the discipline to ship only the ones that carry their weight.

$media.alt: Designer sketching interface wireframes at a desk

children.text: Every project starts with more ideas than it can hold. The first week is generous; the rest of the project is editing. By the time something ships, most of what we made is gone — and the work is better for it.
The one-question test
For every element we ask a single question: if we removed this, would anyone miss it? If the answer is no, it goes. Colour, type, motion, copy — everything gets the same test.
Restraint is a series of small deletions, not one big decision.
The result is work that loads fast, reads clearly, and ages well. It is also the hardest kind of work to sell in a kick-off meeting — which is exactly why it is worth writing down.

data.title: Notes on choosing a type pairing
data.excerpt: One display face, one workhorse. Everything we have learned about pairing type for editorial sites.

$media.alt: Fountain pen resting on handwritten notes

children.text: A type pairing fails for the same reason most design fails: two voices competing for the same sentence. Our rule is simple — one face performs, the other supports, and neither improvises.
Contrast, not competition

A high-contrast serif at display sizes against a neutral sans for everything else gives an editorial voice without noise. Instrument Serif with Inter is the pairing on this very site: quiet where it should be, loud where it must be.
If you can name three reasons a typeface is beautiful, pick the fourth one instead.
Test the pair on real copy — footnotes, captions, error messages — before you commit. Most pairings survive a hero headline; few survive a table of contents.

data.title: The tools we rely on
data.excerpt: A short, honest list of the software that survives every project — and the ones we keep quitting.

$media.alt: Laptop and sketchbook on a wooden desk

children.text: Our stack has shrunk every year. Figma for design, Astro for the web, EmDash for content, and a plain text editor for everything else. Anything that needs a weekly tutorial does not survive the quarter.
What we keep quitting
Project management tools. We have tried all of them, twice. A shared document and a honest weekly call have outperformed every board we ever maintained.
The best tool is the one you stop noticing after a week.
If you are starting out: pick boring tools, learn them deeply, and spend the saved energy on the work itself.

data.title: Editing is the design
data.excerpt: The sentence you cut does more for the layout than any grid ever will.

$media.alt: Open notebook and coffee cup beside a laptop

children.text: We used to treat copy as content that arrives after design. Years of editorial work taught us the opposite: the length of the paragraph decides the rhythm of the page before a single style is applied.
Write with the layout, not for it
Cut a sentence and the white space appears on its own. Shorten a heading and the grid finally breathes. Most layouts we are asked to fix are typography problems wearing a layout costume.
Delete the paragraph and watch the design improve — that is the test.
So now we write first, design second, and the pages are calmer for it. The words were the design all along.

data.title: Designing in public
data.excerpt: Sharing rough work before it is ready feels risky. It is also the fastest feedback loop we have found.

children.text: Polished work gets polite nods. Rough work gets real comments. Posting early drafts — half-typed case studies, unglamorous sketches — has improved our process more than any workshop.
The audience is smaller than you fear
A handful of thoughtful readers beats a large indifferent one. The notes we get from sharing early are specific, generous, and often come from people doing similar work.
Ship the draft. The draft is where the useful feedback lives.

data.title: The case for quiet interfaces
data.excerpt: Interfaces that stop competing for attention are the ones people keep using.

$media.alt: Minimal laptop setup with a single window open

children.text: Loud interfaces win demos and lose mornings. Badges, banners, and motion compete for a budget of attention that was already spent before the page finished loading.
Hierarchy is kindness

A quiet interface is not an empty one — it is an ordered one. One accent, used sparingly; one scale of type; one motion language. The user's eye moves because the layout told it where to go, not because something blinked.
Every element shouting makes the whole page whisper nothing.

data.title: Photography for designers who claim they cannot shoot
data.excerpt: You already compose grids and crops all day. The camera is just another viewport.

$media.alt: Camera and notebook on a table by a window

children.text: Designers already know more about photography than they admit: framing, hierarchy, cropping, the discipline of removing things. The camera is simply another viewport with worse undo.
Three rules that transfer
One light source beats three mediocre ones. Get closer than feels comfortable. And let negative space do the talking — the same generosity that makes a layout breathe makes a photograph.
Shoot what you already look at. The eye you trained on layouts does not lie when it finds a scene.

data.title: Shipping small
data.excerpt: Small releases keep taste in the loop. Big releases only show you what you already broke.

$media.alt: Hand writing a checklist in a notebook

children.text: A release the size of a paragraph can be judged by taste. A release the size of a book can only be judged by test coverage. We ship small so that judgement — the human kind — stays in the loop.
The compounding part
Small ships compound: each one teaches you something about the next. Big ships only teach you what already broke, months after you could have done anything about it.
Momentum is a design material. Ship small enough to keep it.
